name: Fränkel function regulator

lead: The Fränkel function regulator (FR) is a removable orthodontic appliance developed by German orthodontist Rolf Fränkel in the 1950s. Instead of pressing on the teeth, it sits in the space between the teeth and the lips and cheeks, holding the soft tissues away and guiding the tongue and lower jaw. The look-related goal is a better-aligned bite and, in children with a recessed lower jaw (Class II), a more balanced side profile.

It belongs to the family of functional appliances, which orthodontists use during growth. Systematic reviews and randomized trials have compared it with other appliances such as the Twin Block and headgear; the research base is large and the results are discussed as appliance-by-appliance comparisons.

paras: An orthodontist selects one of several FR designs (FR-1 to FR-4, plus later variants) according to the type of bite problem and makes a custom acrylic-and-wire device. Wearers are typically children or young teenagers, and treatment is described as lasting one to two years, usually followed by other orthodontic work or retention. The device is bulky and can affect speech at first.

Reported drawbacks are bulk, speech interference, breakage and dependence on cooperation with wear. Effects on the jaw are most plausible while the patient is still growing. Because it is a custom orthodontic device, it is fitted and monitored by an orthodontist rather than bought off the shelf.

angle.text: In growing children the FR is used to correct bite relationships and jaw position, which changes how the chin and lips sit in profile. It is a prescribed orthodontic treatment rather than a self-directed practice.

lead: The Fränkel function regulator (FR), also called the Frankel appliance, is a removable orthodontic appliance designed by the German orthodontist Rolf Fränkel in the 1950s [1][2]. It is a tissue-borne device made of acrylic shields and wire that sits in the vestibule, the space between the teeth and the lips and cheeks, and is meant to retrain the muscles around the mouth while encouraging the jaws to develop in a more balanced relationship [1][2].

Its link to appearance is the profile and the bite. For a growing child whose lower jaw sits behind the upper (Class II malocclusion), the aim is to bring the lower jaw forward, reduce a prominent overjet and improve how the teeth, lips and chin relate in profile. Variants exist for other patterns, including Class III and open bites [1][2]. Online, the appliance is mentioned in discussions of functional jaw orthopedics and non-surgical jaw growth.

Research on functional appliances is extensive. A 2026 systematic review pooled 90 studies of mandibular length change and counted the Frankel appliance among the most assessed designs (573 patients) alongside the Twin Block [3]. Earlier meta-analyses, randomized trials and comparisons with headgear and with other functional appliances are listed below [4][5][6][7].

paras: The FR is built from acrylic buccal shields and lip pads connected by wire elements. The shields hold the cheeks away from the dental arches, the lip pads keep the lower lip off the front teeth, and wires such as palatal and labial bows give stability [2]. Because the appliance is described as mainly tissue-borne, it avoids heavy contact with the teeth so they can erupt and move under the influence of the surrounding muscles [1][2].

Wikipedia lists five main types: FR-1 for Class I and Class II division 1, FR-2 for Class II divisions 1 and 2, FR-3 for Class III with upper lip pads to encourage upper-jaw growth, FR-4 for open bite and bimaxillary protrusion, and FR-5 for high mandibular plane angles, used with headgear [2].

Fränkel worked in Zwickau, in the former East Germany, and developed the appliance in the 1950s after finding the earlier Activator gave mixed results in his practice [1][2]. His approach drew on the functional matrix theory proposed by Melvin Moss and on earlier functional appliances such as the Andresen activator [1]. Grokipedia reports that it reached the wider orthodontic world after a 1966 presentation to the European Orthodontic Society and later courses and a 1989 book on orofacial orthopaedics with the function regulator [1].

Orthodontic descriptions say treatment is aimed at the mixed-dentition and early pubertal years and involves near full-time wear for one to two years, sometimes combined with fixed appliances before or after [1]. Success is described as depending on patient cooperation [1].

A systematic review published in 2026 evaluated removable and fixed functional appliances in Class II treatment, screening 6,796 records and including 90 studies, four of them randomized controlled trials. The Twin Block (783 patients) and the Frankel appliance (573 patients) were the most commonly assessed [3].

A 2010 meta-analysis in the European Journal of Orthodontics examined mandibular changes during Fränkel-2 treatment compared with untreated growing Class II subjects [4]. Randomized trials include a 1998 comparison of headgear with the function regulator for early Class II division 1 treatment [5] and a 2020 trial comparing the Frankel 2 with the modified Twin Block [6]. A 2024 study used three-dimensional computed tomography to examine airway volume in growing Class II patients treated with the Frankel II [7]. Earlier work, such as a 1983 paper asking whether Fränkel therapy is orthopedic or orthodontic, shows that how much of the change is skeletal and how much dental has long been debated [8].
Grokipedia summarizes outcomes as an average overjet reduction of 4 to 5 mm with a skeletal share of roughly 30 to 40 percent, with results varying by compliance [1].
Reported disadvantages are bulk, temporary speech difficulty, breakage and limited usefulness in patients who do not wear it consistently or who have finished growing [1].
